1156.title: Common prayer
1156.hook: the same prayers said together across the world
1156.howItsDone: In Anglican churches each Sunday and holy day has an appointed collect, prayed near the start of the service, and the prayer book directs the Sunday collect to be used again through the week that follows at Morning and Evening Prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, George Herbert's country parson, out visiting on a weekday. Your line was the ordinary parish.

Why does the Lord's Prayer start with "our"? "Our Father which art in heaven." Jesus could have taught "my Father." Even when someone prays it alone, on the edge of a bed at midnight, the first word is plural. The prayer assumes company. The Church of England put the idea on its prayer book's cover: the Book of Common Prayer. Common, as in shared. The same words, on the same day, in one parish and the next and the next. Today: common prayer.

In Acts, just after Pentecost, the first believers are described like this: "they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." Prayers they kept together. The Greek word behind fellowship there is koinonia: sharing, a life held in common. Common prayer reaches for the same thing. In the prayer book, each Sunday and holy day has its own short prayer called a collect, set out through the whole church year. So on a given Sunday, a village church and a city church miles away pray the same collect. A collect speaks to God, remembers something God has done, asks for one thing, and closes through Christ. Here's the one for the second Sunday in Advent: "Blessed Lord, who hast caused all holy Scriptures to be written for our learning; Grant that we may in such wise hear them, read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest them." Inwardly digest: a whole way of reading in one breath. Some who pray this way describe a quiet gift: on a day with no words of one's own, or no strength to mean them, other voices hold the prayer up, and another day the favor is returned. Jesus makes a promise sized for a small room as much as a cathedral: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Christians pray in more than one way. Some prefer their own words in the moment; churches with a prayer book or set liturgy lean on shared texts. Either way, the first word is still our.

Take this week's collect, or the old one from the communion service: Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid. If you pray, say it slowly, aloud or inside, holding in mind the others saying words like these today, in a cathedral, a hospital chapel, a kitchen; if you don't, simply listen to the words and keep the others in mind.
Common prayer. The same prayers, said together by people who may never meet, from one shared book and one shared year.
Your line: prayer in common. Words shared across many rooms. Go gently.

1157.title: Luther's barber
1157.hook: Luther taught his barber to pray through the Lord's Prayer, Commandments and Creed like a garland
1157.howItsDone: Some Lutherans and other Christians use Luther's method, praying slowly through a commandment, a line of the Creed or a petition of the Lord's Prayer as instruction, thanksgiving, confession and prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, common prayer: the same words, said together. Your line was prayer in common.

A man who cuts hair for a living asks his customer a question that can be hard to ask out loud: how do you actually pray? The customer is Martin Luther. The story goes that Luther answered with a little book, written for, in his words, a good friend, Master Peter the barber. In English it's called A Simple Way to Pray. A famous reformer, writing a how-to for a man with a razor. Today the path moves from the Anglican prayer book to the Lutheran and Reformed ways, and it starts in a barbershop.

Luther starts with honesty. He admits there are days his heart is cold and he has no wish to pray. On those days he takes his little psalter, goes to his room, or to church if people are there, and quietly says the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer and some psalms, the way a child would. Words he already knows by heart. Then he slows down inside them. He takes one commandment at a time and makes of it a garland of four strands. Instruction: what does this teach me? Thanksgiving: what can I thank God for here? Confession: where have I fallen short? Prayer: what do I ask? Take the first commandment: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." Instruction: God asks to be trusted above everything. Thanks: that God offers to be my God at all. Confession: the other things I lean on harder. Prayer: help me trust you. Then he turns to Peter's trade. A good barber keeps his whole mind on the razor and the hair. If he chats and looks around, he may cut someone's mouth, or nose, or throat. Prayer needs the whole heart like that. And then a surprising freedom. If, partway through, a thought catches fire, Luther says, let the rest go and listen. In his words, the Holy Spirit himself is preaching, and that sermon is worth far more than our own prayers. So the method is a trellis, not a cage, there to get a cold heart started, and Luther is glad to see it climbed over.

Take "Thou shalt not steal," or go back to the first commandment, and give each strand a few breaths: what does it teach, what is there to be thankful for, where have I missed it, what would I ask? If you pray, speak the four strands to God; if you don't, let the questions turn over quietly. And if one thought takes hold, follow it, the way Luther told Peter to.
Luther's barber. Master Peter, for whom Luther wrote a simple way to pray: the Commandments, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, woven into garlands of four strands.
Your line: a simple way to pray. Four strands, and room for the Spirit. Until tomorrow.

1158.title: Only comfort
1158.hook: the Heidelberg Catechism begins: what is your only comfort in life and death?
1158.howItsDone: In Reformed churches that use the Heidelberg Catechism, it is taught to young people and new members, and some congregations preach through it in sections called Lord's Days over the course of a year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's barber: four strands through one commandment. Your line was a simple way to pray.

What is your only comfort in life and in death? That's the very first question of a catechism, a book of questions and answers for teaching the faith. It doesn't open with the nature of God or the order of the universe. It opens with the question someone asks at a sickbed, or lying awake in the small hours. The book is the Heidelberg Catechism, named for the German city it came from, and still taught in some Reformed churches. Some learn its first answer by heart and carry it for life.

Here's the answer, put plainly. That I am not my own. That I belong, body and soul, in life and in death, to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ. It goes on: he has paid for my sins and set me free; he watches over me so that not a hair can fall from my head without the Father's will; and by his Spirit he makes me willing and ready to live for him. Comfort here isn't a mood that comes and goes. It's a fact about belonging: whose you are. It starts with a negative, not my own, close to Paul's words: "ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price." To some ears that sounds like a loss. The catechism hears it as relief. If I am not my own, I don't have to hold myself together. Someone faithful is holding me. And to the Romans: "whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's." The hairs of your head echo Jesus in Matthew: "But the very hairs of your head are all numbered." The second question asks what you need to know to live and die in this comfort, and answers in three parts: how great my sin and misery are, how I am set free from them, and how I am to thank God for that freedom. Guilt, grace and gratitude, as some teachers put it, and the rest of the catechism follows that order. Other churches have their own catechisms; Luther wrote a small one too, back on day eight hundred fifty-eight. Heidelberg chose to begin with comfort.
screen: `WHETHER WE LIVE OR DIE, THE LORD'S.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself honestly: what is my comfort, in life and in death? Don't hurry to a right answer; notice what comes up first, a person, a place, a habit, a hope, a blank, and let it be. If you pray, set the catechism's line, I am not my own, beside whatever came up and see how they sit together; if not, stay with the question.
Only comfort. The Heidelberg Catechism's first question, and its answer: I am not my own, but belong to my faithful Savior, in life and in death.
Your line: my only comfort. Belonging, not a mood. That's today, done.

1159.title: The Genevan psalter
1159.hook: Calvin's churches sang the psalms set to rhyme and tune
1159.howItsDone: Reformed and Presbyterian churches sing metrical psalms from psalters, some singing only psalms in worship and others mixing psalms with hymns; "All people that on earth do dwell" to the Old Hundredth tune is sung in churches of several traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, only comfort: the Heidelberg Catechism's first question. Your line was my only comfort.

Psalm one hundred, in the King James Bible: "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands. Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing." Lovely. Now try getting a whole church to sing that together: farmers, children, people who can't read. Prose has no steady beat. Nobody knows when to breathe or where the tune goes next. In Geneva, John Calvin's church found an answer: put the psalms into rhyme and regular meter, so anyone could sing them to one strong tune. Today's word: metrical psalm.
screen: `MAKE A JOYFUL NOISE, ALL YE LANDS.`

segments.voice: A metrical psalm is a psalm rewritten in rhymed verse, with a regular count of syllables in each line, so it fits a tune. Calvin wanted the whole congregation singing in worship, not only trained singers. And for songs to sing to God, he argued, you could not do better than the psalms, words he believed God's Spirit had already given. So poets set the psalms into French verse, and musicians fitted them to simple, sturdy tunes. The result was the Genevan Psalter. The idea traveled. English Protestants who had lived in Geneva carried it home, and one of them, William Kethe, set Psalm one hundred like this: "All people that on earth do dwell, / Sing to the Lord with cheerful voice." Eight syllables a line. That steady count lets a crowd move together, breathing in the same places. His words were sung to a tune from the Genevan psalter, and the pairing came to be called the Old Hundredth. Kept from the psalm: all ye lands becomes all people on earth; gladness becomes a cheerful voice. Changed: now it rhymes, and a child can remember it after a few Sundays. Paul told the Colossians to be "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." Churches read that line in more than one way. Some Reformed and Presbyterian churches sing only psalms in worship. Others sing psalms alongside hymns. Either way, the metrical psalm put the Bible's own songbook into ordinary mouths.
screen: `ALL PEOPLE THAT ON EARTH DO DWELL.`

segments.voice: If you know the tune, sing the first two lines of the Old Hundredth, all people that on earth do dwell, sing to the Lord with cheerful voice; if not, say them slowly and tap the eight beats of each line on your knee. Then sit in the quiet after the last note. If you pray, let the two lines be your prayer; if you don't, notice what it's like to put your one voice into words whole rooms have sung together.
Metrical psalm. A psalm set in rhyme and steady meter, so a whole congregation can sing it to one tune.
Your line: all people that on earth. One steady beat, and a whole room can sing. See you tomorrow.

1160.title: Puritan meditation
1160.hook: Richard Baxter taught heavenly meditation: thinking deeply on one truth
1160.howItsDone: Some Reformed and evangelical Christians meditate in the Puritan way: they choose a verse or a truth, think it through slowly, speak to their own hearts about it, and turn it into prayer, often in a daily quiet time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, psalms set in rhyme so a whole church could sing. Your line was all people that on earth.

"There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God." One short verse from the letter to the Hebrews. An English Puritan pastor named Richard Baxter built a long book on it, called The Saints' Everlasting Rest. The story goes that he began it while badly ill and far from home, expecting to die, with little to read but his Bible. He lived, and the book became a guide to a kind of prayer he called heavenly meditation: taking one truth and thinking it through until it reaches the heart. Today: Puritan meditation.
screen: `A REST TO THE PEOPLE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Baxter noticed something in believers, himself included: you can know a truth perfectly well and feel nothing about it. Heaven becomes a doctrine on a shelf. Meditation, for him, was carrying a truth from the head down to the heart, work he called consideration. Pick one truth; for Baxter it's usually the rest God promises. Don't skim it. Turn it over. What is this rest? Who is it for? What would it be like to be finished with grief and striving? Then let it stir you: love, desire, hope, joy. And when your own heart is slow, talk to it. Baxter calls this soliloquy, preaching to yourself, and he points to the psalmist: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God." He isn't speaking to God there, or to a friend, but to his own soul, arguing it back toward hope. The word Hebrews uses for that rest is sabbatismos: a sabbath-keeping. Not a nap. A sabbath, like the rest the letter says God took on the seventh day, now held open for his people. The Bible's first psalm already blesses this habit: "in his law doth he meditate day and night." In this tradition, meditation isn't emptying the mind. It's filling it with one thing and staying there. Christians meditate in other ways too, with an image, a single word, or silence. The Puritans kept close to a text, reasoned with it, and talked back to their own hearts.
screen: `WHY ART THOU CAST DOWN, O MY SOUL?`

segments.voice: Choose one line, there remaineth a rest to the people of God, or another that matters to you, say it once, and turn it over: what does it say, and what would it mean if it were true for you today? When your mind wanders, come back to the line, and if your heart feels slow, try Baxter's way and speak to it. If you pray, end by bringing the line to God.
Puritan meditation. Taking one truth, like the rest God promises, and thinking it through until it moves from the head to the heart.

1161.title: Family worship
1161.hook: Reformed and Puritan homes read and prayed together daily
1161.howItsDone: In some Reformed, Presbyterian and other Protestant homes, families keep daily family worship: reading a passage of scripture, singing a psalm or hymn, and praying together, often after a meal or before bed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one truth carried from head to heart. Your line was the saints' everlasting rest.

A poem by Robert Burns follows a Scottish farm laborer home at the end of the week. Supper is over. The family pulls in around the fire. The father takes down the big family Bible, the one that was his own father's pride, and lays his cap aside. They sing a psalm. Then, Burns writes, "The priest-like father reads the sacred page." And he prays. A poet's picture, and a tender one. But in Reformed and Puritan homes, a scene like that wasn't meant for one Saturday night. It was meant for every day.

Reformed Christians found the idea in the Bible. Moses tells Israel to keep God's words on their hearts, and "teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Home, road, bed, morning: faith spoken at the kitchen table, not only at the altar. Joshua says it in one line: "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." And Paul greets Priscilla and Aquila and "the church that is in their house." A household could be a small church. The Church of Scotland set out a directory for worship at home: households were to pray together, read the scriptures, and sing praises, with the head of the house leading. The shape was simple: a psalm sung, a chapter read, a question or two for the children, a prayer. It doesn't wait for Sunday, or for the minister. The father or mother who was arguing over the bills an hour ago now opens the book. The children who fidgeted through supper hear the same stories their grandparents heard. And for a few minutes the kitchen becomes a place of worship. Not every home looked like Burns's poem, and homes now look all kinds of ways: a single parent and a teenager, roommates, a couple, a grandmother and one grandchild. Some Christians keep the old pattern with a devotional book at breakfast. Some pray together at bedtime. The furniture changes. The idea stays: a household that stops, together, and turns toward God.
screen: `THE CHURCH THAT IS IN THEIR HOUSE.`

segments.voice: If someone is nearby, ask whether you can read them something short, like Psalm one twenty-one: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." If you're alone, read it aloud anyway, keeping in mind the people you share a roof or a table with, or once did. Then sit quietly a moment, and if you pray, name each of them before God.
Family worship. A household stopping together at home to read scripture, sing and pray: the house as a small church.
Your line: the household at prayer. Home, road, bed and morning, each a place to turn toward God. Good night.

1162.title: The Lord's Day kept
1162.hook: Scottish Presbyterians kept a quiet, holy Sunday
1162.howItsDone: Christians gather for worship on Sunday, the Lord's Day. In the Scottish Presbyterian tradition the whole day was kept for church, Bible reading, rest and works of mercy; Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday as the Sabbath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, family worship: a household reading and praying together at the table. Your line was the household at prayer.

It's the first day of the week, in Troas, and the church has gathered in an upstairs room to break bread. Paul is leaving in the morning, so he talks until midnight. A young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window, sinks into a deep sleep, falls from the third loft, and is taken up dead. Paul goes down, embraces him, and says his life is in him. Then he goes back upstairs, breaks bread, and talks until daybreak. A glimpse, from Acts, of Christians gathering on the first day.

The Gospels say the empty tomb was found on the first day of the week. Christians came to gather on that day, and in Revelation, John writes, "I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day." Scottish Presbyterians, heirs of the Reformed way this week has followed, kept all of it. Their Westminster Confession calls it the Christian Sabbath: rest from ordinary work and from recreations, the whole day given to worship, in church and at home, with room for works of necessity and mercy. In homes that kept it this way, the Sunday clothes came out, in some the meal was made the day before, and the hours went to church, the Bible, the catechism, a quiet walk, a visit to someone ill. From outside it could look stern. To those who loved it, it was a day the rest of the week couldn't touch. Behind it sits the old commandment, "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy," and Isaiah's picture of people who "call the sabbath a delight." Christians keep the day in different ways. Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday, the seventh day, as the Sabbath. Others hold that in Christ every day belongs to God, and keep Sunday for worship without the full Sabbath rules. Jesus himself said, "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Jewish neighbors keep their own Sabbath on the seventh day. This week walked through common prayer, Luther's garland for his barber, an only comfort, psalms in rhyme, a long meditation, a family at the table. It ends with a whole day handed back.

Keep a small sabbath right now: phone face down, out of reach if you can, shoulders dropped. For these minutes nothing needs answering, fixing or finishing, and any task that floats up can wait; it will still be there. If you pray, give these minutes to God; if you don't, simply rest in them.
The Lord's Day kept. Sunday, the first day of the week, set apart whole for rest, worship and mercy, the way Scottish Presbyterians kept it.
Your line: a day set apart. A whole week, ending in a whole day. Until tomorrow.
